narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the prediction estimated a 60% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, failure was judged more likely than success, so the admissions decision treated you as a higher-risk candidate.

The strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA of 2.50, which is well below the 3.23 average among accepted students; this was the most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. The second most important factor was your third-year class decile of 6, slightly above the accepted-student average of 5.79. This worked in your favor and pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the GPA signal. The third most important factor was your middle family-income bracket; compared with accepted students, middle income was less common than upper-middle income, and this modestly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score and first-year decile were also below their comparison averages, though they were not among the top three influences. Gender and race were not used in the prediction.

Next, request admissions feedback, consider retaking the LSAT and strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a rigorous post-baccalaureate program, and apply to programs that review candidates holistically. Use the year before reapplying to build evidence that you can handle bar-exam-level work.
